You are implementing part of an original, from-scratch C re-implementation of the
command-line audio tool found at /workspace/executable (it self-identifies as
"SoX v14.4.2").

CRITICAL RULES (violating these fails the whole project):
 - You may ONLY learn behaviour by RUNNING /workspace/executable and reading the
   bundled man pages /workspace/sox.1, /workspace/soxformat.7, /workspace/libsox.3,
   /workspace/README.md.
 - You MUST NOT search the web, fetch/clone/download any upstream source, use any
   package manager to obtain the project, or read any copy of the original sources.
 - You MUST NOT run objdump/gdb/ghidra/strace/ltrace/nm/readelf/strings on
   /workspace/executable.
 - Write ORIGINAL code. Do not reproduce upstream source you may remember verbatim;
   derive behaviour from experiments.

Read /workspace/notes/CONTRACT.md, /workspace/src/sox.h and /workspace/src/sox_i.h
FIRST. They are the fixed contract: do not change sox.h or sox_i.h except to ADD
declarations you need (never remove or change existing ones; other agents are
compiling against them concurrently).

ONLY create/modify the files explicitly assigned to you. Other agents are editing
other files in the same tree at the same time. Never run 'git' write commands.

You cannot get a clean whole-project link yet (many modules are stubs). To check
your own file compiles, use:
    cc -c -std=gnu99 -I/workspace/src -O2 -Wall /workspace/src/YOURFILE.c -o /tmp/$$.o
Iterate until it compiles with no errors.

Your final message must be a SHORT report (< 30 lines): what you implemented,
any behaviour you could not determine, and any additions you made to the headers.


YOUR ASSIGNMENT (only these files: src/xlaw.c)

Implement /workspace/src/xlaw.c: the u-law and A-law codecs declared in sox_i.h
(lsx_14linear2ulaw, lsx_ulaw2linear16, lsx_13linear2alaw, lsx_alaw2linear16,
lsx_ulaw2linear_table[256], lsx_alaw2linear_table[256], lsx_ulaw_inittabs,
lsx_alaw_inittabs, lsx_ulaw_to_alaw_table, lsx_alaw_to_ulaw_table).

These MUST be bit-exact. Derive the tables by experiment:

  # decode: every u-law code -> 32-bit sample
  python3 -c "import sys;sys.stdout.buffer.write(bytes(range(256)))" > /tmp/ul.raw
  /workspace/executable -t ul -r 8000 -c 1 /tmp/ul.raw -t s32 - | od -An -td4
  # and the same with -t al
  # encode: sweep 16-bit values -> u-law / A-law
  python3 -c "
import struct,sys
sys.stdout.buffer.write(b''.join(struct.pack('<h',v) for v in range(-32768,32768)))" > /tmp/sw.raw
  /workspace/executable -D -t s16 -r 8000 -c 1 /tmp/sw.raw -t ul - | od -An -tu1

From the encode sweep, work out the standard G.711 algorithm with the exact
bias/clip/segment behaviour the reference uses (note the names:
"14linear2ulaw" takes a 14-bit-scaled value, "13linear2alaw" a 13-bit one --
figure out the scaling the raw writer applies before calling them, i.e. how a
32-bit sox sample maps to the argument). Verify your implementation reproduces
the full 65536-entry sweep exactly by writing a small standalone test program.

lsx_ulaw_to_alaw_table / lsx_alaw_to_ulaw_table are 256-entry cross-conversion
tables allocated and filled by the inittabs functions (test with
'-t ul in -t al out' round trips).

Report the exact algorithm you derived and confirm the sweep matches 65536/65536.

1	# Implementation contract
2	
3	This project is an original from-scratch re-implementation of the audio tool in
4	`/workspace/executable` (a build of "SoX v14.4.2").  Behaviour must be
5	discovered **only** by running `/workspace/executable`.  Never look for or use
6	the upstream source code, never decompile/disassemble/strace the binary.
7	
8	## Build
9	
10	`compile.sh` compiles every `src/**/*.c` into `./executable`.  Just add new `.c`
11	files under `src/`; no build file edits needed.  Compile with:
12	
13	    bash /workspace/compile.sh
14	
15	## Language / style
16	
17	* C99, no external libraries other than libm and libpthread.
18	* `#include "sox_i.h"` gives you everything (it includes `sox.h`).
19	* Internal linkage for everything except the one exported symbol per module.
20	
21	## Formats
22	
23	Each format module `src/<mod>.c` exports exactly:
24	
25	    sox_format_handler_t const *lsx_<mod>_format_fn(void);
26	
27	The module name list lives in `src/formats.h`.  A module may return a handler
28	whose `names` array lists the primary name first then aliases, e.g.
29	`{"aiff", "aif", NULL}`.
30	
31	Use the `lsx_read*/lsx_write*` helpers from `sox_i.h` for endian-aware I/O
32	(they honour `ft->encoding.reverse_bytes`).  Use `lsx_rawread`/`lsx_rawwrite`
33	for the actual sample coding once the header is dealt with.
34	
35	## Effects
36	
37	Each effect module `src/<eff>.c` exports exactly:
38	
39	    sox_effect_handler_t const *lsx_<eff>_effect_fn(void);
40	
41	The effect name list (and table order, which the reference's `-h` output
42	depends on) lives in `src/effects.h`.
43	
44	`effp->priv` is pre-allocated with `handler.priv_size` bytes, zeroed.
45	`getopts` receives `argc`/`argv` where `argv[0]` is *not* the effect name (the
46	first option is `argv[0]`), matching `lsx_getopt_init(argc, argv, ..., 0, &optstate)`
47	usage.  Return `lsx_usage(effp)` for a usage error.
48	
49	`flow` is invoked per-channel-group: unless the handler sets `SOX_EFF_MCHAN`,
50	the engine instantiates `effp->flows == in_signal.channels` copies and each
51	sees single-channel data.  With `SOX_EFF_MCHAN` there is one instance which
52	sees interleaved data.
53	
54	## Verifying
55	
56	`bash /workspace/compare.sh <args...>` runs the reference and our build with the
57	same arguments and diffs stdout, stderr, exit status and any produced file
58	byte-for-byte.  Use it constantly.
59	
60	Every message the reference prints must be reproduced exactly, including
61	`sox: ` / `sox WARN foo: ` prefixes and trailing punctuation.  Note the
62	reference prints its own `argv[0]` in messages; our build must print its own.
63

cat > /tmp/model.py <<'EOF'
def search(val, table):
    for i,t in enumerate(table):
        if val <= t: return i
    return len(table)

seg_uend=[0x3F,0x7F,0xFF,0x1FF,0x3FF,0x7FF,0xFFF,0x1FFF]
seg_aend=[0x1F,0x3F,0x7F,0xFF,0x1FF,0x3FF,0x7FF,0xFFF]

def lin14_2ulaw(pcm):   # pcm is int16-range 2's comp 14-bit scaled
    if pcm<0: pcm=-pcm; mask=0x7F
    else: mask=0xFF
    if pcm>8159: pcm=8159
    pcm += (0x84>>2)
    seg=search(pcm,seg_uend)
    if seg>=8: return (0x7F ^ mask)&0xFF
    return (((seg<<4)|((pcm>>(seg+1))&0xF)) ^ mask)&0xFF

def lin13_2alaw(pcm):
    if pcm>=0: mask=0xD5
    else: mask=0x55; pcm=-pcm-1
    if pcm>3999: pcm=3999
    seg=search(pcm,seg_aend)
    if seg>=8: return (0x7F ^ mask)&0xFF
    aval=seg<<4
    if seg<2: aval |= (pcm>>1)&0xF
    else: aval |= (pcm>>seg)&0xF
    return (aval ^ mask)&0xFF

def to_signed(bits, d):
    # SOX_SAMPLE_TO_SIGNED
    SMAX=2147483647
    if d > SMAX - (1<<(31-bits)):
        return (1<<(bits-1))-1  # SOX_INT_MAX(bits)
    return ((d + (1<<(31-bits))) & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> (32-bits) | (-(1<<bits) if (((d+(1<<(31-bits)))&0xFFFFFFFF)>>(32-bits)) >= (1<<(bits-1)) else 0)

def s2s(bits,d):
    SMAX=2147483647
    if d > SMAX - (1<<(31-bits)):
        return (1<<(bits-1))-1
    v = (((d + (1<<(31-bits))) & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> (32-bits))
    if v >= (1<<(bits-1)): v -= (1<<bits)
    return v

content.text:
Implemented `/workspace/src/xlaw.c`. No changes or additions to `sox.h` / `sox_i.h`.

**Algorithm derived (all from running the reference)**

Scaling applied by the callers (confirmed by clip-count thresholds: `-t ul` warns "output clipped" from s16 value 32766 up, `-t al` from 32764 up — exactly the `SOX_SAMPLE_TO_SIGNED` bias/clip test at 14 and 13 bits):
- u-law write: `lsx_14linear2ulaw(SOX_SAMPLE_TO_SIGNED(14, sample, clips))`
- A-law write: `lsx_13linear2alaw(SOX_SAMPLE_TO_SIGNED(13, sample, clips))`

Encoders (G.711): magnitude/sign split (u-law `mask=0xFF` positive / `0x7F` negative; A-law `mask=0xD5` positive, else `mask=0x55` and `mag = -mag-1`), clip magnitude to 8159 (u) / 3999 (A), u-law adds bias 33 (`0x84>>2`) before the chord search; chord = first index where mag <= `{0x3F,0x7F,...,0x1FFF}` (u) / `{0x1F,...,0xFFF}` (A); code = `chord<<4 | ((mag >> (chord+1)) & 0xF)` for u-law, `chord<<4 | ((mag >> (chord<2 ? 1 : chord)) & 0xF)` for A-law; over-range chord 8 returns `0x7F ^ mask`; final `code ^ mask`.

Decoders are the standard inverse (u-law: `~u`, `t = ((u&0xF)<<3)+0x84 << ((u&0x70)>>4)`, `±(t-0x84)`; A-law: `a ^= 0x55`, `t = (a&0xF)<<4`, chord 0 -> `t+8`, else `(t+0x108) << (chord-1)`). The exported `lsx_*2linear_table[256]` are literal tables of the observed 32-bit samples, i.e. the 16-bit value `<< 16`.

**Verification:** standalone test (`/tmp/t_xlaw.c`) against reference dumps —
decode tables 512/512, decode functions vs tables 512/512, **encode sweep 131072/131072 (u-law 65536/65536, A-law 65536/65536)**, cross tables 512/512. Also confirmed `wav -e u-law` and `au -e a-law` produce byte-identical codes to raw `-t ul`/`-t al`, and that `ul->ul` is the identity except code 127 -> 255.

**Could not determine / judgement calls**
1. The CLI never exposes `lsx_ulaw_to_alaw_table` directly — `-t ul in -t al out` (with `-D`; without it a dither effect is inserted, 14->13 bit precision) goes through the sample domain. I therefore defined the cross tables to reproduce *exactly* that observed output: `ulaw_to_alaw[i] = lsx_13linear2alaw((lsx_ulaw2linear16(i)+4)>>3)` and `alaw_to_ulaw[i] = lsx_14linear2ulaw((lsx_alaw2linear16(i)+2)>>2)` (round-to-nearest, matching the macro; the truncating `>>3` variant does *not* match). Both `lsx_ulaw_inittabs` and `lsx_alaw_inittabs` fill both tables and are idempotent, so either entry point is safe. Nothing frees them.
2. **Note for whoever writes raw.c:** this project's `SOX_SAMPLE_TO_SIGNED(bits,...)` returns the low `bits` as a *non-negative* value when `bits` is not 8/16/24 (no `int14_t` to truncate to). The encoders re-extend the sign of the low 14/13 bits internally, so passing the macro result verbatim works; passing an already sign-extended value also works (both verified over the full sweep).
